reader.summary: Indonesia faced a dual crisis this week. The worst forest and peatland fires in eleven years continued to rage, with monitors reporting nearly two million hectares burned and toxic haze blanketing Indonesia and neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia. President Prabowo accused foreign media of "insulting" the country while domestically anti-government protests erupted over land-clearing practices. Dozens of orangutans were rescued, and Singapore issued further haze notices to Indonesian firms. Simultaneously, Indonesian financial markets suffered a severe rout after MSCI issued a double downgrade warning that could strip the country of its emerging-market index status, threatening roughly $65 billion in passive fund inflows. The central bank held its key rate, Prabowo accused MSCI of "intimidation," and Indonesia moved to exclude tightly held stocks from its benchmark index ahead of a Monday meeting with MSCI. Other notable events included a four-nation "Badr" defence pact with Qatar, Turkey and Pakistan, a record drug seizure of over two tonnes of ketamine and methamphetamine, a ferry fire with all passengers rescued, and a nine-per-cent cut in pipeline gas exports to Singapore.

key_events.event: MSCI issued a double downgrade warning threatening to exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes, triggering a multi-day market rout that pushed equities to a six-year low.
Worst forest and peatland fires in eleven years burned nearly two million hectares, producing toxic haze across Southeast Asia and prompting anti-government protests.
Indonesia announced it would remove tightly held, high-concentration stocks from its benchmark index starting November 2 to avert MSCI exclusion.
Indonesia, Qatar, Turkey and Pakistan signed the 'Badr' defence cooperation pact, deepening multi-lateral military ties.
Bank Indonesia held its key policy rate but hiked the deposit facility rate, describing the move as part of a broader 'policy mix' to support the rupiah and growth.
Indonesian police seized over two tonnes of narcotics, including 1.16 tonnes of ketamine and 1.2 tonnes of methamphetamine, in one of the country's largest drug busts.
A ferry caught fire near an Indonesian port; all passengers and crew were evacuated and rescued.
Indonesia cut pipeline gas exports to Singapore by roughly nine per cent.
Singapore expanded its haze crackdown, issuing notices to three additional Indonesian companies linked to fire emissions.
Dozens of orangutans were rescued from the fires and released into a protected forest.

display.eli5:
Indonesia is dealing with two big problems at the same time. First, massive forest fires are burning through the peatlands in the east, and the smoke is so thick that it drifts over Singapore and Malaysia, making the air toxic there. Second, a big international stock-rating company called MSCI is threatening to kick Indonesia out of its emerging-market list, which would mean billions of dollars of automated investment money flowing out of the country.

Next week, the most important event is the MSCI meeting. Indonesia has already made some changes to its index to try to win them back, so the meeting will probably soften the warning but not fully cancel it. The fires will ease a bit as some rain comes, but the haze and the angry protests about land-clearing will stick around. Prabowo, the president, is also dealing with his own team turning on him over the free meals programme, right around his two-year anniversary in office.

If the sovereign wealth fund Danantara suddenly dumps a huge amount of money into buying Indonesian stocks, that would be a genuine surprise and would temporarily prop up the market. That is the kind of thing nobody is expecting but that would change the whole tone of the week.
